## Before we start

Welcome to your first CS5701 RStudio lab! This document is an R Markdown file - a mix of text (like this) and grey "chunks" of R code that you can run.

- To run a chunk, click the small green play arrow at the top-right corner of the chunk, or place your cursor inside it and press **Ctrl+Enter** (Windows) / **Cmd+Enter** (Mac).
- The output (numbers, tables, plots) appears directly underneath the chunk.
- You don't need to install anything for the core material today - the only extra package used anywhere in this document is `ggplot2`, and only in the stretch sections below.
- If you haven't already installed R and RStudio, see the Week 0 material on Brightspace.

A few common first-time hiccups, in case you hit them:

- **"object ... not found"** - usually a typo in a name, or an earlier chunk hasn't been run yet. Chunks generally need to run top to bottom, in order.
- **"could not find function"** - a function may belong to a package that hasn't been loaded yet with `library(...)`.
- **"cannot open file / connection"** - R is looking in the wrong folder for a file. We'll cover this in the "Reading in a csv file" section below.

Don't worry about memorising any of this now - we'll point it out again as we go, and we (and the GTAs) are here to help.

**This is the extended version of today's lab.** It contains everything in the core walkthrough, plus optional **Stretch challenge** sections (marked like this one) are best suited to pathway B. These are entirely optional: work through the core material at your own pace first, and dip into the stretch boxes whenever you like, in any order. If you chose pathway A today you can always come back and try the stretch challenges in your own time.

## 1. Describing Data

Both during the QDA lecture and in the pre-reads material, we introduced measures of location and spread. Now let's practice computing them using R.

### 1.1 Measures of location

We'll start with a small vector of numbers:

```{r}
data_vector <- c(4, 7, 2, 5, 6, 2)
```

A quick note on what just happened: `c()` combines values into a single vector, and `<-` stores ("assigns") the result under a name we chose - here, `data_vector`.

#### Mean

```{r}
mean(data_vector)
```

#### Median

```{r}
median(data_vector)
```

Do these values match what you'd get applying the definitions from the lecture by hand?

#### Mode

Unlike the mean and median, R has no built-in function for the mode (the most frequently occurring value).

> **Stretch challenge: write your own mode function**
>
> Hint: turn the vector into a table of frequencies (`table()`), then find the category with the highest count.
>
> ```{r, eval=FALSE}
> mode_fn <- function(v) {
>   # your code here
> }
> ```

<details>
<summary>Click for one possible solution</summary>

```{r}
mode_fn <- function(v) {
  freq_table <- table(v)
  as.numeric(names(freq_table)[which.max(freq_table)])
}

mode_fn(data_vector)
```

Note: this simple version only returns one value even if there's a tie for most frequent. A further challenge: adapt it to return *all* the tied values.

</details>

#### Weighted mean

You'll have seen in your induction talks (and in Brunel's Senate Regulations 3 and 4) that your grade point average takes into account the credit-weighting of each module. Here's what that calculation looks like in R:

```{r}
grade.point <- c(13, 16, 12)
credit <- c(15, 15, 30)
weighted.mean(grade.point, credit)
```

You don't need this for QDA itself, but it may come in handy later in the year!

### 1.2 Measures of variation

#### Range

```{r}
range(data_vector)
```

This returns the minimum and maximum value.

#### Interquartile range (IQR)

```{r}
IQR(data_vector)
```

This is based on the 25th and 75th percentiles, which you can also compute directly:

```{r}
quantile(data_vector, c(0.25, 0.75))
```

#### Standard deviation and variance

```{r}
sd(data_vector)
```

```{r}
var(data_vector)
```

#### All of the above, in one go

```{r}
summary(data_vector)
```

`summary()` returns the minimum, 25th percentile, median, mean, 75th percentile and maximum in one line - a quick way to get an overview of any numerical variable.

## 2. Exploring a Real Dataset

So far we've used numbers we typed in ourselves. In practice, data usually arrives as a file - most commonly a `.csv`.

### Reading in a csv file

- Download `worms.csv` from Brightspace.
- Save it in the **same folder** as this `.Rmd` file. By default, R looks for files relative to the folder this file is saved in - if `worms.csv` isn't there, you'll get a "cannot open file" error.
- Run the chunk below to read the data in:

```{r}
worms <- read.csv("worms.csv")
```

Check what the data looks like:

```{r}
head(worms, n = 10)
```

### Numerical summaries of categorical variables

Recall from the lecture that the numerical summary for a categorical variable is a frequency table. This is straightforward in R:

```{r}
table(worms$Vegetation)
```

You can also cross-tabulate two categorical variables at once, creating a contingency table:

```{r}
table(worms$Damp, worms$Vegetation)
```

Try swapping in other columns from `worms` to explore further.

> **Stretch challenge: relative and cumulative frequency**
>
> Build the full frequency table from the lecture - frequency, relative frequency, and cumulative frequency - for `Vegetation`:
>
> ```{r}
> freq <- table(worms$Vegetation)
> rel_freq <- prop.table(freq)
> cum_freq <- cumsum(freq)
>
> data.frame(
>   Frequency = as.vector(freq),
>   Relative.Frequency = round(as.vector(rel_freq), 2),
>   Cumulative.Frequency = as.vector(cum_freq),
>   row.names = names(freq)
> )
> ```
>
> Do these numbers match what we built by hand in the lecture?

### Graphical summaries for categorical variables

A bar chart shows the frequency of each category:

```{r}
barplot(table(worms$Vegetation))
```

(Use the Help pane - type `?barplot` into the Console - to see how you could add a title to this plot.)

### Graphical summaries for numerical variables

#### Histogram

A histogram shows the distribution of a numerical variable:

```{r}
hist(worms$Worm.density, xlab = "Density", ylab = "Count", main = "Distribution of Worm Density")
```

#### Box plot

A box plot is useful for comparing a numerical variable across categories:

```{r}
boxplot(worms$Worm.density ~ worms$Damp)
```

From this plot: is the median worm density higher when the soil is damp, or when it isn't? Which group has the larger spread?


> **Stretch challenge: using ggplot2**
>
> `ggplot2` is a widely-used, more flexible plotting package - you may already have met it if you used R in a previous module.
>
> ```{r}
> library(ggplot2)
> ```
>
> (If it isn't already installed on this machine: Tools -> Install Packages, or use the Packages tab.)
>
> Reproducing the bar chart, histogram and box plot above:
>
> ```{r}
> ggplot(worms) + geom_bar(aes(x = Vegetation), fill = "steelblue") +
>   labs(title = "Vegetation from the Worms data") +
>   theme_classic()
> ```
>
> ```{r}
> ggplot(worms, aes(x = Worm.density)) +
>   geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue") +
>   labs(title = "Histogram of Worm Density") +
>   theme_bw()
> ```
>
> ```{r}
> ggplot(worms, aes(x = Worm.density, y = Damp)) +
>   geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue2") +
>   labs(title = "Box Plot of Worm Density by Damp") +
>   theme_classic() +
>   coord_flip()
> ```
>
> A pie chart needs a little more setup - the frequency table has to be turned into a data frame first:
>
> ```{r}
> w1 <- table(worms$Vegetation)
> w2 <- as.data.frame(w1)
> colnames(w2) <- c("Vegetation", "Frequency")
>
> ggplot(w2, aes(x = "", y = Frequency, fill = Vegetation)) +
>   geom_bar(width = 1, stat = "identity") +
>   coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
>   labs(title = "Pie Chart for Vegetation in the Worms data")
> ```
>
> There's a lot more `ggplot2` can do - see this [cheatsheet](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/master/data-visualization-2.1.pdf) for an overview.
